note: Size budgets for the built output. Checked by `npm run budget`, enforced in CI.
`limit` is a ceiling somebody chose. `measured` is what the build produced when
the limit was last recorded, kept beside it so the headroom is visible without
running anything. Refresh the measurements with `npm run budget:update`; that
command deliberately does NOT touch the limits.
Raising a limit is a commit with a reason. The limits below were set at the
first measurement (2026-08-14, commit b066c89) with roughly 5% headroom on the
text bundles and the asset trees. demo-css-gzip is the exception: at 7 KB, 5%
is 360 bytes and one new component's classes would trip it, so it carries a
flat ceiling instead of a percentage.

limits below are raised to fit the code that exists; whether an unminified
bundle is the right thing to publish is a separate question and a separate
change. Do not raise these again without asking it.
A2 RAISED lib-esm-gzip, and only that one. It went 0.4 KB over; lib-iife-gzip
did not go over and is deliberately left where it is, at 1.7% headroom, rather
than pre-emptively widened. A limit raised before it is breached is slack the
change did not earn - see the P6 note above - and A3 tripping this one is the
forcing function the paragraph above asks for, not an accident to smooth over.
Re-measured while raising it, and the ESM figure is worse than the IIFE one:
106.1 KB gzipped of which 55.4 KB - 52.2% - is comments. Two observations that
should shape the answer rather than delay it further:
- The IIFE is the bundle a browser downloads as written. Its 37.6% is a real
cost paid by every end user of a drop-in <script> tag.
- The ESM entry is consumed through a bundler, which strips comments on the
consumer's way to production. Its 52.2% is a transfer-and-parse cost at
install and build time, not a runtime cost - and those comments are the
JSDoc that gives a typed consumer its documentation and hover text.
So the two entries plausibly want different answers, and 'minify the library'
is the wrong shape of question. Still not this sprint's decision to make.

texture-vram is the third KIND of budget in this file, after P6's per-file

ones already here. 202 images weigh 5.23 MB on disk and occupy 164 MB of GPU

every other line here. That is what a phone runs out of, not the download.

is skipped, so the number can only under-report, which is the safe direction
for a ceiling to sit on. KTX2/Basis is the answer and B1 did not ship it: the
encoder needs KTX-Software binaries that are not installed here, and quoting a
published ratio instead of measuring one is the thing this program refuses to
do. The arithmetic that IS measurable says BC7/ETC2 would take 164 MB to 41.

texture-vram is at 72% headroom and is deliberately NOT lowered to 5%. The

back to RGBA8, and the figure would climb back toward 43 MB. The headroom is
that fallback, and tightening it would make the budget fail on the hardware it
is least able to help.

=== J2 TASK ONE: THE DEPLOY-SIZE DECISION ===
public-total RAISED 11,180,000 -> 16,770,000 and demo-total 19,990,000 ->
29,985,000. Both exactly 1.5x, taken as a decision BEFORE any acquisition
runs, which is what RM-012 J2's acceptance gate asks for. The item count is
the OUTPUT of this, not its input - the same substitution RM-011 W-4 made
when it withdrew H1's `about ninety materials` as a number.
WHAT THE CEILING BUYS. 5,843,561 B of headroom against a measured catalog
mean of 27,997 is 209 items; against the median of 11,218 it is 521. RM-007
asks for 400-600, so this ceiling reaches the top of that range ONLY if
packs come in near the median, and a heavy pack has to be trimmed or
refused. That is the point rather than an accident: X-2 measured that
curation is the lever and compression is not - 152 of 168 models are already
Draco and 11 already KTX2, so a pack will not come in under the mean by
being encoded harder. A ceiling with the whole growth pre-authorised inside
it would notice nothing, which is the argument against 2.0x.
WHAT WAS MEASURED FIRST, because none of it turned out to bind. Cloudflare
Pages on the free plan allows 20,000 files a site and 25 MiB a file; the
deployed tree is 626 files and its largest asset is 307 KB, and at 600 items
it would be about 1,490. The build takes 1.44 s against a 20-minute timeout.
A visitor downloads the same 400.3 KB either way, because J1 made a pack a
fetch and first-load is unmoved by anything in public/ that nobody opens.
The one permanent cost is git, measured at 1.13x the bytes added on H1's
material library - 4,504,845 raw bytes for a 5,072,108-byte pack delta. That
is 53 -> 60 MiB at this ceiling, and history does not shrink.
So the ceiling is self-imposed, and it should be: the line that actually
protects a visitor is first-load, and it is untouched. This one protects the
decision instead - it makes the next acquisition somebody's choice.

=== J2: PACKS ARE FETCHED, NOT BUNDLED ===
catalog-index is RE-POINTED and RENAMED catalog-bundled, 3,940 -> 2,600 with
3,553 -> 2,451 measured. This is not a lowering and the distinction is the
same one RM-011 H1 drew when it re-pointed texture-vram: the number under
the line is a different number. catalog-index measured
src/catalog/catalog-index.json, and that file no longer exists - J2 took
every catalog row out of the bundle. What is bundled now is a manifest of
four packs plus the three generated sections, which name no model file and
so cannot be in a pack. The line still answers the question J1 gave it:
what catalog content does a visitor download before asking for any of it.
The comparison worth recording is not 3,553 against 2,451, because the old
number never counted the generated sections. Like for like, the catalog in
the payload went 5,429 -> 2,451 gzipped: the index (3,553) plus openings,
stairs and structures (1,876), against a 575-byte manifest plus the same
1,876. A 2,978-byte saving, which is real but is not the point.
The point is what the number is a function of. The old line grew by ~34
gzipped bytes for every row added, so X-3 could project it to 20,611 at 600
rows and 17,264 bytes of first-load growth against 13,292 of headroom. The
new one grows by ~90 bytes when a KIT is acquired and by nothing at all when
an item is. Acquiring 200 chairs moves it by one line. That is why the
limit is set at 2,600 rather than left where it was: a ceiling with the old
line's growth pre-authorised inside it would notice nothing, and this line
exists to make catalog content entering the payload a decision somebody
records.
catalog-packs is ADDED as the thirteenth line, at 10,450 with 9,935
measured. J2 moved a cost rather than removing one. Every row is fetched
now, which is what keeps first-load flat while the catalog grows - but the
bytes went somewhere, and where they went is the first click on the
furniture button. public-total counts them at rest on a disk and first-load
correctly ignores them; nothing was asking what a person waits for the
first time they go looking for a chair. Now something is.
Set at the usual ~5 % deliberately, and it WILL be raised when a pack is
acquired - that is the ratchet working rather than failing. The number to
watch is not the total but what it buys: 9,935 gzipped bytes for 168 rows
across two tiers is 59 bytes a row, so RM-007's 600 rows is about 35 KB of
drawer-open. Worth a wait; worth knowing about; not worth discovering.
